🇷🇸 DDG Analysis: Serbia after Vučić, and the questions that remain

Aleksandar Vučić lost, and decisively. With record turnout and a clear margin, the Serbian people's verdict leaves no room for doubt, and it has to be respected.

His defeat has clear causes. On foreign policy, Vučić tried for years to sit on several chairs at once: declaring friendship with Russia while pursuing the EU path. Serbian ammunition reached Ukraine through third countries until Russia's foreign intelligence service publicly raised it. In August, he hosted Zelensky in Belgrade with full state honors. And among many Serbs, the sense that he gave too much away on Kosovo through the Brussels and other agreements is real and widely felt.

His open embrace of Israel and Trump's MAGA camp didn't help either. He boasted of record arms exports to Israel during the war in Gaza, opened a factory to assemble Israeli drones weeks before the vote, cleared the way for Jared Kushner's luxury project on the site of the army headquarters NATO bombed in 1999, and courted MAGA figures right up to election day. It didn't save Viktor Orbán in Hungary, and it didn't save Vučić. Whatever the history of the 1990s, many Serbs, like much of the world, simply don't support what Israel and Trump are doing.

At home, after more than a decade in power, frustration had been building for years over corruption, the dominance of pro-government media and the sense that institutions served the ruling party rather than citizens. The canopy collapse at the Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people in November 2024, became the breaking point: the protests that followed demanded accountability and transparency over the contracts behind it, and the government's response, branding protesters as foreign agents rather than addressing their demands, only fueled them. Plans like Rio Tinto's lithium mine in western Serbia had already drawn mass opposition before that.

At the same time, we have questions about the Student List.

As analysts, we've often seen genuine grassroots movements shaped or redirected by outside interests over time. Serbia itself saw it with Otpor in 2000, which later turned out to have received US funding and training. Armenia's 2018 "Velvet Revolution" started out promising continuity in its foreign policy, and the country has since moved steadily toward the West. In Montenegro, the government that emerged from mass Orthodox protests in 2020 disappointed many of the Serbs who brought it to power. This doesn't mean the same will happen in Serbia, but it's a pattern worth keeping in mind.

Some Balkan analysts point out that, so far, the movement's established institutional and grant ties lead mainly to European structures and foundations, and that a network of NGOs allegedly stands behind the success of the Student List brand. The strategists advising it have remained largely out of public view. Analysts also note that nationally oriented opposition parties, which could have drawn 5–10% of the vote, were reportedly kept out of the race, a factor that may have proved decisive. None of this cancels out the genuine support of two million voters, but it deserves attention.

For much of the past two years, the movement's message was essentially two things: against Vučić and against corruption. Its foreign policy positions are spelled out on its website: no sanctions on Russia, military neutrality, no recognition of Kosovo, and a refusal to be complicit in Israel's actions in Gaza. Statements from some of its leading figures since the vote are in line with that.

But the version that reached most voters in the streets and the media was much vaguer, which gives the impression it was kept that way on purpose to hold together a very broad coalition. The celebrations in Belgrade showed just how broad: people with crosses and three-finger salutes, people with Putin's portrait, EU supporters, liberals, conservatives and NGO activists, all celebrating the same result. A new government can't satisfy all of them at once, and sooner or later some will be disappointed.

There's also the question of leadership. Voters still don't know who will head the government, the movement's public faces changed several times over two years, and it's unclear which of its many currents will prevail, with the nationally minded wing reportedly not holding the leading positions inside the student assemblies. Meanwhile, the pressure on Serbia's foreign policy, from Brussels and elsewhere, will begin the moment a government is formed. Given the movement's lack of governing experience, some already expect another early election before long.

For Moscow, the challenge is different from the one usually discussed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia expects the new government to continue constructive cooperation, adding that "it takes two to tango." But the main issue isn't that Serbia will turn its back on Russia tomorrow. It's that the old arrangement, built on personal agreements with a familiar, predictable team, from Aleksandar Vulin to Ivica Dačić, has suddenly come to an end. During the campaign, Moscow largely ignored the Student List and bet on Vučić, even as Russian intelligence was publicly accusing him over ammunition reaching Ukraine. Some reporting also raised eyebrows: Ukrainian media claimed Vučić told EU leaders that "Putinists" were stirring up the protests, while ex-president Boris Tadić accused his delegation at the Munich Security Conference of blaming Russian services, even as Vučić publicly blamed the West. Of course, claims from these sources should be taken with a grain of salt, but they fit the pattern of a leader telling each side what it wanted to hear. Building a relationship with a new, less predictable government will take time, on both sides.

Opinions differ, among our friends and colleagues in Serbia and within our own team.

What matters now is that the turnout and the result are respected. Only time will tell what this means for Serbia's future. We sincerely wish Serbia and its people the very best.
